questions.text: A 300 mm beam contains two 80 mm conduits with spacing of 240 mm center-to-center. Check compliance with NSCP spacing and size limits.

options.text: Both spacing and size compliant, assuming no additional structural constraints are present
Size non-compliant (exceeds h/3 = 100 mm) and spacing adequate (240 mm = 3 × 80 mm).
Spacing non-compliant (240 mm < 3 × 80 = 240 mm), which may require adjustment
Cumulative area exceeds limit; both conduits must be reduced, or alternative solutions considered

rationale.a: While size is compliant, spacing is exactly at the limit (not 'adequate' with margin).
rationale.c: 240 mm = 3 × 80 mm, so spacing meets the minimum requirement.
rationale.d: Cumulative area = π(40)² × 2 ≈ 10,053 mm² > 7,854 mm² (h/3 equivalent for 300 mm), so cumulative exceeds limit.
rationale.correct: Beam size limit = h/3 = 300/3 = 100 mm. The 80 mm conduits are individually compliant (80 < 100 mm). Spacing requirement = 3 × 80 = 240 mm. Actual spacing = 240 mm, which equals the requirement (compliant, just at the limit) (NSCP 6.3.1 & 6.3.2). The size criterion is satisfied, but the spacing is right at the boundary.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A 350 mm × 350 mm column requires a 110 mm diameter utility sleeve. Is this within the 4% embedded area limit, and if so, what is the maximum area in mm²?

options.text: Non-compliant; 110 mm conduit exceeds 4% area limit. Maximum allowed is 4,900 mm².
Compliant; conduit area ≈ 9,503 mm² is within the 4,900 mm² limit, ensuring structural integrity and compliance with building codes
Compliant; the 110 mm conduit is less than h/3 of the column dimension, maintaining the necessary structural proportions
Cannot determine without knowing the reinforcement ratio of the column, which affects the overall structural capacity

rationale.b: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.c: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.d: This option is incorrect. Review the correct answer above.
rationale.correct: Column area = 350 × 350 = 122,500 mm². Maximum embedded = 4% × 122,500 = 4,900 mm². A 110 mm diameter conduit has area = π(55)² ≈ 9,503 mm². Since 9,503 mm² > 4,900 mm², the conduit exceeds the 4% limit and is non-compliant (NSCP 6.3.1).
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: Two electrical conduits (25 mm diameter each) are embedded in a concrete slab. What is the minimum center-to-center distance between them per NSCP?

rationale.c: 100 mm = 4 × diameter (more than required; acceptable but not minimum).
rationale.d: 25 mm is the conduit diameter itself (no spacing).
rationale.correct: Minimum spacing between adjacent conduits is 3 times the conduit diameter, measured center-to-center (NSCP 6.3.2). For 25 mm conduits: 3 × 25 = 75 mm.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A slab has ribbed joists (rib width = 120 mm). What is the maximum diameter of electrical conduit that can be embedded in the rib per NSCP?

rationale.a: 40 mm = w_rib/3, which is NOT the code limit for ribs.
rationale.c: 60 mm = w_rib/2 (far too large for slender ribs).
rationale.d: 20 mm is more conservative than required.
rationale.correct: For ribs in ribbed/joist slabs, the maximum conduit size is w_rib/4 = 120/4 = 30 mm (NSCP 6.3.1). This tighter limit (vs. h/3 for solid slabs) applies because ribs are slender and sensitive to voids.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015 § 6.3.1 (Ribbed Slab — rib conduit limit w_rib/4)

questions.text: A beam (400 mm deep) requires a utility sleeve (110 mm diameter) that exceeds the standard size limit h/3 ≈ 133 mm. Wait—actually, is 110 mm within the limit? If yes, is it compliant? If no, what is required?

options.text: Compliant; 110 mm is within the h/2 limit.
Non-compliant; only conduits ≤ 50 mm are allowed without reinforcement.

rationale.b: 110 mm is NOT greater than 133 mm; it is within the limit.
rationale.c: h/2 = 200 mm is not the code limit; h/3 is the limit.
rationale.d: The limit is h/3 (which equals 133 mm here), not a fixed 50 mm.
rationale.correct: For a 400 mm beam, h/3 = 400/3 ≈ 133 mm. The 110 mm conduit is less than 133 mm, so it is compliant with the size limit (NSCP 6.3.1). No supplemental reinforcement is required.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A 400 mm × 400 mm concrete column is to be analyzed for embedded utility pipes. What is the maximum total area of embedded pipes per NSCP?

rationale.c: 16,000 mm² = 10% of column area (far too large).
rationale.d: 4,800 mm² = 3% of column area (below 4% but not the code value).
rationale.correct: For columns, the maximum embedded area is 4% of the gross cross-sectional area (NSCP 6.3.1). Column area = 400 × 400 = 160,000 mm². Max embedded = 0.04 × 160,000 = 6,400 mm² (ERR-STRC-024).
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A 250 mm deep beam requires embedded HVAC ducts. The largest single duct proposed is 90 mm diameter. Is this compliant per NSCP, and if not, what is the maximum allowed?

options.text: Compliant; 90 mm < 250 mm, which is a common misinterpretation of the code
Compliant; 90 mm is within the h/2 limit, which is not applicable in this context
Non-compliant; maximum allowed = 75 mm (h/3.3), which is a miscalculation of the standard

rationale.a: Compliance is not simply 'less than full depth'; the h/3 rule is the code limit.
rationale.c: h/2 = 125 mm is not the code limit; the limit is h/3.
rationale.d: The correct formula is h/3 ≈ 83 mm, not h/3.3.
rationale.correct: For beams, maximum conduit size = h/3 = 250/3 ≈ 83 mm (NSCP 6.3.1). The proposed 90 mm exceeds this limit. The duct must be reduced to ≤83 mm, or reinforcement must be added around the opening.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A concrete slab (200 mm thick) has four 30 mm diameter electrical conduits running parallel. Assuming they are equally spaced in the slab cross-section, is the cumulative area within NSCP limits?

options.text: Yes, cumulative area = 2,827 mm² is within limits.
No; 200 mm slab allows only one 67 mm conduit (h/3), not four 30 mm conduits.
Yes, if spacing between conduits is ≥ 90 mm (3 diameters).
No; four conduits exceed the h/3 limit regardless of individual sizes.

rationale.b: The h/3 rule applies to total void area, not just single conduit. Multiple smaller conduits can fit if cumulative area is within limits.
rationale.c: While adequate spacing (90 mm) is required, the area check is the primary limit.
rationale.d: The cumulative area is the controlling factor, not the count. Four smaller conduits can be acceptable if total area ≤ h/3 equivalent.
rationale.correct: Four 30 mm conduits have cumulative area = 4 × π(15)² ≈ 2,827 mm². The slab allows up to h/3 ≈ 66.7 mm equivalent diameter, which is ≈3,490 mm² area. Since 2,827 mm² < 3,533 mm², the design is within limits (NSCP 6.3.1). Also, if spacing is ≥3 diameters = 90 mm, the spacing criterion is satisfied.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.text: A 180 mm thick concrete slab in an exterior building has a metal utility conduit (60 mm diameter) embedded for weather-exposed piping. What is the minimum concrete cover to this pipe per NSCP?

rationale.a: 25 mm is not a standard cover in NSCP.
rationale.b: 40 mm applies to interior (protected) elements, not weather-exposed.
rationale.d: 75 mm is for concrete cast against earth (not applicable here).
rationale.correct: Pipes exposed to weather require 50 mm concrete cover minimum, equivalent to the cover for ≥20 mm bars in weather exposure (NSCP 6.3.3 & 6.7.1). This applies because the slab surface and pipe are subject to weathering.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.

questions.code_citation: NSCP 2015 § 6.3.3 (Cover for Embedded Pipes — weather exposure)

questions.text: A 150 mm thick concrete slab has electrical conduits embedded. What is the maximum diameter of a single conduit per NSCP?

rationale.b: 75 mm = h/2, which exceeds the h/3 limit.
rationale.c: 100 mm approaches the full slab thickness and is far too large.
rationale.d: 30 mm is smaller than allowed (conservative but not standard).
rationale.correct: For slabs and beams, the maximum conduit size is h/3 = 150/3 = 50 mm (NSCP 6.3.1). This ensures the void does not overly weaken the concrete section.
rationale.takeaway: Review the correct answer and associated code provision.
